aboutAuthor: Saurabh Mukherjea, Rakshit Ranjan, and Salil Desai lead research at Marcellus Investment Managers in Mumbai. Diamonds in the Dust distills their consensus-driven stock-picking system for consistent Indian equity compounding.

points.heading: Consistency beats brilliance
points.body: Most investors chase spectacular wins and end up with erratic returns. Marcellus's philosophy targets modest but repeatable compounding — 15–20% annually sustained for decades turns small sums into fortunes. The math of consistency outperforms bursts of genius.

points.heading: Look for clean accounts, not exciting stories
points.body: The team screens for forensic red flags: receivables growing faster than sales, frequent 'other income', promoter pledging, and auditor churn. Companies with spotless accounting survive downturns; those with creative books rarely give your capital back.

points.heading: Franchise quality shows up in cash flow
points.body: A great franchise converts profit into free cash flow year after year without needing constant capital infusions. Return on capital consistently above the cost of capital is the single clearest marker of durable competitive advantage.

points.heading: Concentrate on the obvious winners
points.body: Rather than owning fifty average businesses, hold ten to fifteen dominant franchises with honest promoters — the 'diamonds in the dust'. Concentration in high-quality names, not diversification into mediocrity, drives long-term outcomes.

points.heading: Do nothing is a strategy
points.body: Portfolio turnover destroys returns through costs, taxes, and missed rebounds. Once the quality case holds, the best action is usually no action. Wealth creation is mostly about sitting still while good businesses compound.

points.heading: Behavioral discipline is the real edge
points.body: The authors show that Indian retail investors systematically buy tops and sell bottoms. A written process — screening rules, review cadence, pre-committed responses to drawdowns — protects you from your own emotions when markets test them.

insights: The book's 'Coffee Can' lineage comes from Mukherjea's earlier bestseller The Unusual Billionaires.
Marcellus runs every stock idea through a monthly consensus meeting where dissent is mandatory.
Forensic accounting screens flagged several famous Indian corporate collapses years before they happened.
conclusion: Diamonds in the Dust argues that extraordinary wealth is built by ordinary discipline: clean accounts, cash-generative franchises, concentration in quality, and the patience to do nothing. Compounding rewards character more than cleverness.
